Perkins' original caption: "The Southern Hotel in Old Newhall: This famous old hostelry, reputed to be the finest hotel between Los Angeles and San Francisco, was built in 1877 by Henry M. Newhall. In 1887 the hotel was so badly damaged by a disastrous fire that it was never rebuilt. It was at the corner of Market and Main Streets, now Railroad Avenue." (Note: In other places, Perkins uses 1878 for the hotel's establishment. It was probably constructed during 1877 and opened in early 1878 when the town of Newhall completed its move to this location.) Click image for more.

Perkins writes: "The first successful commercial oil refinery erected in California was located in Newhall." The two larger stills remain; as of 2013 they're located on property off of Pine Street that Chevron USA (aka Standard Oil) donated to the city of Santa Clarita. Click image for more.

Camping here in 1769, Fr. Crespí considered the Santa Clarita Valley "a very suitable site for a Mission." Click image for more information.

Mission San Fernando was erected in 1797. In 1804, church officials established an estancia, or outpost, on a bluff overlooking today's junction of Interstate 5 and Highway 126. Click image for more information.

Detail from panoramic photograph of Castaic Junction on March 18, 1928, showing flood damage from the St. Francis Dam. Published in Charles Outland's "Man-Made Disaster" (1963/77). Shown is the location of the milk house, which still stood (at left); and the estancia, or Mission outpost, which was in ruins (identified here as an asistencia, or sub-mission, which it probably wasn't). Today, Interstate 5 would be in the foreground and Highway 126 would run off to the right. Click image to enlarge.

We know of two different diseños of the Rancho San Francisco that were drawn. There may have been more. It seems a new map was drawn whenever boundaries were challenged in court, a frequent occurrence in the mid-1800s. Click image to see more.

One of two markers placed at the dedication of the Oak of the Golden Dream on March 9, 1930 (the 88th anniversary of the Lopez discovery) — this one on the tree itself. Perkins includes this photograph with the published version of this story, saying in the photo caption: "Both plaques were stolen and the Lopez plaque came back. The other plaque is still missing." Shown here is the "other" plaque referred to; the Lopez plaque can still be seen at the base of the tree where it's cemented into a monument. Click image to see more.

William Lewis Manly, 29, and John Rogers, 22, broke camp Nov. 4, 1849, to find civilization. They found it at the Del Valle family home, on the Rancho San Francisco, near present-day Magic Mountain, on Jan. 1, 1850. Fed and clothed, they returned to Death Valley with supplies — and a proven route out of the wilderness. Click image for more information.

Overland stage (celerity) wagon of a type that would have seen use on the trails through the Rancho San Francisco in the 1850s and 1860s. Click image for more information.

While progress had its way with the rest of the Rancho San Francisco, Camulos maintained a sense of the pastoral life of its old Spanish days, as romanticized in Helen Hunt Jackson's influential 1884 novel, "Ramona." Click image to enlarge.

Sanford Lyon was bured in the family plot, known as the Pioneer Cemetery, which was located near Lyon's Station. About 1958 (after Perkins wrote this story), when Eternal Valley Cemetery was established, Sanford's and the other long-negelcted graves were moved a short distance to the new Garden of Pioneers. Click image for more information.
